claims.claim: Keeping task-relevant information in a stable, visible external store, rather than in working memory, improves performance on the concurrent task, at the cost of weaker memory for the offloaded content.
A checklist or reference card kept at hand reduces omissions in multi-step or rule-governed tasks compared with relying on memory.

player-aid.helps: when a session uses conventions worth keeping in view but not worth memorising; external stores free working memory in lab tasks, and reference aids are used to cut omissions in procedural work, though the evidence is mixed and large checklist studies in surgery disagree
player-aid.backfires: when the aid replaces judgement, or stands in for conventions the person never learns, since people remember less of what they expect to be able to look up

claims.claim: Stating at the outset the specific question a session must answer improves the relevance and focus of the work, compared with starting without a stated goal.
claims.construct: goal specificity; advance organisers; learning objectives

claims.claim: Having one's smartphone within reach, even silent and face down, reduces available cognitive capacity, and moving it to another room restores that capacity.
claims.construct: the "brain drain" / mere-presence effect of smartphones

claims.claim: Ending a work session in the middle of a unit of work, such as mid-sentence, rather than at a natural break, increases the likelihood and ease of resuming the work at the next session.
claims.construct: the resumption tendency after interruption (Ovsiankina effect); the Zeigarnik effect

claims.claim: Leaving a visible cue of where you were and what comes next at the point of interruption reduces the time and errors involved in resuming a task.

cover.helps: when the sitting needs one question to aim at; stating the goal first is supported only by related work on advance organisers, so treat the question as the contract to check the return against, not a guarantee of focus
cover.backfires: when an early, narrow question locks in the wrong problem, when moving the phone away causes more anxiety than its presence did (the phone-presence effect failed a direct replication), or when stopping mid-sentence is not paired with a written note of the next step

claims.claim: Separating idea generation from evaluation, with judgement deferred until generation is done, increases the number of ideas without reducing, and sometimes increasing, the number of good ones.
Instructing people to generate deliberately bad ideas lowers self-censorship and yields more ideas, including some usable ones, than instructing them to generate good ideas.
claims.construct: lowered quality criterion; instruction effects in divergent thinking

claims.claim: In a single idea-generation run, later ideas tend to be more original than earlier ones.
claims.construct: the serial order effect in divergent thinking

ten-bad-ideas.helps: when wanting a good idea is what stops the first one being written; later ideas in a run tend to be a little more original, a small tendency that is unreliable for any one person, and asking for bad ideas is untested craft, so treat the ten as a warm-up and read the later boxes first
ten-bad-ideas.backfires: when "bad" turns into jokes rather than range, or when ten is too few to get past the obvious answers: the studies of later ideas being more original used timed runs of several minutes

claims.claim: Exposure to randomly selected stimuli (words or prompts unrelated to the problem) during idea generation increases the number and originality of ideas, compared with generating without stimuli.
claims.construct: random entry / external stimulation in idea generation

claims.claim: Deliberately combining two distant concepts produces more original ideas than working from a single concept, with originality driven by attributes that emerge from the combination.

forced-connections.helps: when ideas have gone stale and familiar; outside stimuli can lift idea output, but random words themselves are untested, so treat each connection as a prompt to test, not a finding
forced-connections.backfires: when a stimulus fixes attention on itself instead of widening it, as provided examples do in design studies, and during convergence, where unrelated input is noise

claims.claim: Impasses in problem solving are overcome when the solver relaxes a self-imposed constraint on the solution, so deliberately removing a constraint makes new solution paths available.
Separating idea generation from evaluation, with judgement deferred until generation is done, increases the number of ideas without reducing, and sometimes increasing, the number of good ones.

constraint-removal.helps: when an unexamined assumption is blocking every option; dropping a self-imposed constraint breaks impasses in puzzle studies, but removing a real constraint on purpose has not been tested
constraint-removal.backfires: when the constraint was doing useful work: constraints can raise creativity as well as lower it, and an idea designed without the constraint may not survive its return

claims.claim: Exposure to randomly selected stimuli (words or prompts unrelated to the problem) during idea generation increases the number and originality of ideas, compared with generating without stimuli.
claims.construct: random entry / external stimulation in idea generation

claims.claim: Prompting idea generation with generic transformation heuristics ("reverse it", "make it 10×", "borrow from another field") increases the variety and creativity of generated concepts, compared with unprompted generation.
claims.construct: design heuristics / transformation operators; analogical transfer

claims.claim: Impasses in problem solving are overcome when the solver relaxes a self-imposed constraint on the solution, so deliberately removing a constraint makes new solution paths available.

stimulus-die.helps: when the same few ideas keep recurring during a divergent phase; heuristic prompts reduced fixation in one design study, and rolling operators at random is otherwise untested
stimulus-die.backfires: when the face rolled does not fit the problem, when the prompt itself becomes the fixation, and during convergence or evaluation, where random input is noise

claims.claim: Setting a creative problem aside for a break, then returning to it, increases solutions or ideas compared with working on it continuously for the same total time.

Incubation benefits are larger (a) after a longer preparation period, (b) with longer breaks up to a point, and (c) when the break is filled with a low-demand activity rather than rest or a demanding task.
Walking, compared with sitting, increases divergent-thinking output during the walk and shortly after it.
claims.construct: walking / acute physical activity and divergent thinking

claims.claim: Sleeping between first exposure to a problem and a later retest increases the likelihood of discovering a hidden solution or rule, compared with an equal period awake.

step-away.helps: when an open-ended problem has had a proper first pass: setting it aside for a real break, filled with something easy and different, helps on average, more for generating ideas than for insight puzzles
step-away.backfires: when the break is a few minutes of scrolling or other demanding work, when the first pass was too short to have anything to incubate, or when the problem is easy or well-structured

claims.claim: Scoring options on explicit criteria and combining the scores mechanically gives more consistent and more accurate judgements than an unaided holistic judgement.
claims.construct: linear models and decomposition vs holistic (clinical) judgement

claims.claim: A number written or seen earlier pulls later numeric judgements towards it, so a gut score written *before* criteria scoring cannot be anchored by the total.

options-criteria.helps: when options are already on the table and a gut feel may be steering; mechanical totals beat unaided judgement in prediction studies by a small margin, and writing the gut score first keeps the total from pulling it, but on a personal decision the value is the gap between the two, which has not been tested
options-criteria.backfires: when the criteria are chosen or reweighted after a favourite has formed, so the total is built to agree with the gut, when analysing reasons pushes the choice towards whatever is easy to put into words, or when the gut score written first pulls the criteria scores towards it

claims.claim: Imagining that an outcome has already happened ("it failed") leads people to generate more, and more specific, reasons for it than imagining that it might happen.
Running a pre-mortem on a plan reduces overconfidence in it and surfaces more risks than a standard critique or pros-and-cons review.
claims.construct: the pre-mortem as a debiasing technique

pre-mortem.helps: when a plan is about to be locked in; imagining it has already failed surfaced more and better risks than brainstorming in a few team studies, though whether it lowers overconfidence on a solo page is untested
pre-mortem.backfires: when the page pushes for many failure reasons, since struggling to list them can make failure feel less likely, or when explaining one imagined failure in detail makes it seem more probable than the alternatives

claims.claim: Explicitly listing the assumptions a plan depends on, and naming a test for each, identifies more of the plan's vulnerabilities than reviewing the plan without such a list.

Coarse, three-level confidence ratings discriminate correct from incorrect judgements above chance (resolution), even though people are typically overconfident in absolute terms. Items marked low-confidence are therefore a useful flag for risk.
Asking people to consider reasons their judgement could be wrong reduces overconfidence and biased assimilation, compared with no instruction or an instruction to be unbiased.

assumption-audit.helps: when a plan rests on beliefs nobody has written down; listing assumptions is practitioner craft with no direct test, and the evidence that asking for a reason each could be wrong reduces overconfidence is mixed, so treat the low-confidence dots as a guide to which to test first, not a correction
assumption-audit.backfires: when the falsifier column asks for many reasons against each assumption, since listing many is hard and can strengthen the original belief, or when a high-confidence dot is read as proof, because certainty runs ahead of accuracy

claims.claim: Placing items on a spatial layout defined by two explicit dimensions makes their relative standing on both dimensions easier to judge and compare than a list or table does.
Items placed inside the same bounded region are perceived as belonging together, even against other grouping cues, so labelled zones make category membership readable at a glance.
claims.construct: the Gestalt principle of common region (perceptual grouping)

matrix-2x2.helps: when items need comparing on two values at once; laying them on two axes is diagram craft with no direct test, so treat the quadrants as a prompt to argue with, not a measurement
matrix-2x2.backfires: when an axis does not discriminate and everything crowds one quadrant, or when "nothing on a line" forces a false either-or; neither risk has been studied, and in classroom studies the gains from graphic organisers did not carry over to later tasks

claims.claim: Iteratively asking "why?" from a symptom reaches a cause which, when addressed, prevents recurrence more reliably than unstructured problem discussion.

five-whys.helps: when the stated problem is probably a symptom; descending by "why" is manufacturing craft with no controlled test, so treat the bottom rung as a hypothesis to test this week
five-whys.backfires: when the chain stops at an arbitrary depth, settles on one cause for a problem with several, or ends by blaming a person; in hospital root-cause work, repeated analyses mostly produced weak fixes and the same events recurred

claims.claim: Distributing a fixed budget of tokens across options makes trade-offs and opportunity costs explicit, and yields more differentiated priorities than rating each option independently.
claims.construct: constant-sum allocation vs. independent ratings; opportunity-cost neglect

claims.claim: Physically rearranging external objects to think, rather than to reach a physical goal, reduces the cognitive cost of a problem and improves or speeds its solution compared with manipulating the same elements mentally.
claims.construct: epistemic action; interactivity in problem solving

tokens.helps: when a trade-off is abstract and every option could be rated highly; a fixed budget forces the differences that ratings let people skip, and cues to consider what a choice displaces shift decisions, though that effect is small and physical tokens themselves are untested
tokens.backfires: when there are too many quantities to tokenise, or when a token count is read as a measurement rather than a rough allocation; neither has been studied

claims.claim: Making explicit probability forecasts and then receiving outcome feedback or scores improves calibration over successive rounds.
claims.construct: calibration training; forecasting with scoring rules

claims.claim: After an outcome is known, people misremember their earlier probability estimates as closer to the outcome than they were. A dated, written prediction removes that memory distortion when the forecast is scored.
claims.construct: hindsight bias (the memory-design "I knew it" effect)

claims.claim: Starting a prediction from the base rate for its reference class ("how often does this kind of thing happen?") improves forecast accuracy compared with starting from the specifics of the case.
claims.construct: the outside view / reference-class forecasting; base-rate neglect

claims.claim: A number written or seen earlier pulls later numeric judgements towards it, so a gut score written *before* criteria scoring cannot be anchored by the total.

forecast.helps: when a prediction will resolve before the next return; a dated written probability stops hindsight rewriting what you believed, a moderate and well-replicated bias, but learning calibration from a handful of scored forecasts is untested
forecast.backfires: when forecasts are judged by how they turned out rather than by the probability given, a robust bias that affects even people who say outcomes should not count, when too few forecasts are scored to learn from, or when the base-rate line is written and then ignored as not applying to this case

claims.claim: Reconstructing one concrete recent instance of a problem behaviour link by link, and locating the specific point where a different response was possible, identifies a better intervention point than an abstract account of the problem.
claims.construct: behavioural chain analysis; functional analysis of a single episode

claims.claim: Forming written if-then plans ("When situation X arises, I will do Y") increases goal attainment compared with forming a goal intention alone.

frame-by-frame.helps: when the same everyday slip keeps recurring and one recent instance can be recalled in detail; chain analysis is clinical craft never tested on its own, though thinking concretely about an episode is linked to less rumination than thinking about it abstractly
frame-by-frame.backfires: when the reconstruction drifts from what happened into why this always happens to you, the abstract kind of dwelling linked to rumination and low mood

claims.claim: Writing down unfinished tasks and concerns, with at least a next step for each, reduces their intrusion into attention during later work. Listing them without any plan does not.
claims.construct: the cognitive effects of unfulfilled goals; offload by plan-making

claims.claim: When people freely list what they know or think about a domain, the items they list earlier and more often are the ones most salient to them.

Keeping task-relevant information in a stable, visible external store, rather than in working memory, improves performance on the concurrent task, at the cost of weaker memory for the offloaded content.

brain-dump.helps: when unfinished tasks keep intruding on the work, and each item gets a specific next step written beside it; in the lab, making a specific plan, not just a list, is what quietened unfinished goals (one research group)
brain-dump.backfires: when items are listed with no next step, which left the goals active in the one study that tested it, and when the read-back takes what was recent for what matters most: free lists favour recently used items

claims.claim: Physically rearranging external objects to think, rather than to reach a physical goal, reduces the cognitive cost of a problem and improves or speeds its solution compared with manipulating the same elements mentally.
claims.construct: epistemic action; interactivity in problem solving

claims.claim: Having people sort items into their own groups reveals the categories and dimensions they actually use, including ones they cannot readily state.
Items placed inside the same bounded region are perceived as belonging together, even against other grouping cues, so labelled zones make category membership readable at a glance.
claims.construct: the Gestalt principle of common region (perceptual grouping)

card-sort.helps: when the categories are real but unstated and placing each card forces a choice; sorting shows which categories a person uses, and moving physical pieces helped in a few small problem-solving studies
card-sort.backfires: when printed column headings impose categories that are not the person's own, or the finished piles look tidier than the thinking behind them; neither risk has been tested

claims.claim: Building a concept map, made of nodes joined by labelled links, improves understanding and retention compared with reading, listing or outlining the same material.
Drawing a diagram of the causal relations in a problem improves causal reasoning about it compared with reasoning from text alone.
claims.construct: learner-generated diagrams and drawing; causal mapping

node-map.helps: when many parts, causes or players relate and the shape is unclear, and every arrow carries a specific verb such as causes, blocks or needs; building concept maps aids retention of studied material, but it is not a substitute for recalling it
node-map.backfires: when vague links like "relates to" stand in for real relations, when a finished map feels like understanding without being checked, when it grows too dense to read back from a photo, or when it replaces retrieval practice, which beat concept mapping as a study method

claims.claim: Items placed inside the same bounded region are perceived as belonging together, even against other grouping cues, so labelled zones make category membership readable at a glance.
claims.construct: the Gestalt principle of common region (perceptual grouping)

zones.helps: when cards, notes or tokens need a labelled home on the page and the categories are genuinely distinct; items inside the same box tend to be seen as a group
zones.backfires: when the categories are not really distinct, so the zones freeze a premature taxonomy and manufacture false tidiness, and when an item sits across a border and its zone becomes ambiguous

claims.claim: Retrieving studied material from memory (for example, writing down everything you can recall with the book closed) improves retention at a delay of days or more, compared with spending the same time restudying it.

Checking recall against the source right after retrieving it increases the retention benefit and corrects errors that would otherwise persist. Without feedback, errors produced during recall tend to be retained.
claims.construct: feedback in test-enhanced learning; self-scoring accuracy

claims.claim: Errors a person made with high confidence are more likely to be corrected on a later test, once feedback is seen, than errors made with low confidence.
Trying to answer questions about material before studying it, even when most answers are wrong, improves later retention of that material compared with studying it without a pretest.

Coarse, three-level confidence ratings discriminate correct from incorrect judgements above chance (resolution), even though people are typically overconfident in absolute terms. Items marked low-confidence are therefore a useful flag for risk.

free-recall.helps: when studied material has to last days or weeks: writing out what you remember with the book closed, then checking it against the source in a second colour, beats rereading for the same time on a later test, by a small to moderate margin in this free-recall format, though not on a test minutes away
free-recall.backfires: when so little comes back that there is nothing to check, or when the check pass is skipped or scored loosely: errors recalled without correction tend to persist, and people marking their own recall credit wrong answers unless they check it idea by idea

claims.claim: Prompting learners to explain to themselves why each step of given material follows improves understanding and transfer, compared with studying the same material without such prompts.

For novices, studying worked examples whose final steps are progressively removed (completion problems) improves learning compared with unaided problem solving. The advantage shrinks or reverses as expertise grows.
claims.construct: the worked-example effect with fading, and the expertise-reversal effect

claims.claim: Prompting learners to answer "why is this true?" for stated facts improves recall of those facts compared with reading them.

self-explain.helps: when working through stepwise material you are learning: prompts to explain why each step follows improve learning across a range of conditions, though evidence for transfer, for classroom use and for retention after a delay is thinner
self-explain.backfires: when the material already comes fully explained: given explanations crowded out learners' own and lowered learning, while making them feel they had learned more

claims.claim: People overestimate how well they understand how things work. Attempting a step-by-step explanation lowers that self-rating, which exposes the gap.
Explaining material to an imagined novice in one's own words improves understanding and retention compared with restudying it.
Attempting an answer yourself before being given one improves later understanding and retention, compared with receiving the answer first.
claims.construct: the generation effect; productive failure (problem solving before instruction)

feynman.helps: when you feel you understand how something works: trying to explain the mechanism step by step reliably lowers people's rating of their own understanding, which shows where the gap is
feynman.backfires: when the page gets a list of reasons or opinions instead of a mechanism, which did not reduce the illusion, or when the exposed gap is taken for learning: in pre-registered replications, explaining changed people's ratings of their understanding but not their views

claims.claim: Attempting an answer yourself before being given one improves later understanding and retention, compared with receiving the answer first.
claims.construct: the generation effect; productive failure (problem solving before instruction)

claims.claim: Keeping task-relevant information in a stable, visible external store, rather than in working memory, improves performance on the concurrent task, at the cost of weaker memory for the offloaded content.

question-queue.helps: when a question can wait until the page has been worked: trying an answer yourself before being told improves later understanding on average, though deferring an AI's answer has not itself been tested
question-queue.backfires: when the parked question blocks the work on the page, or when the material is new and complex enough that working without guidance costs more than it teaches, as it did for young learners and for domain-general skills

claims.claim: Practice transfers to a target skill to the extent that the practice's cues and required actions resemble the target's. A study method that exercises a different process from the one the test or task demands transfers poorly.
claims.construct: transfer-appropriate processing; identical elements; near vs far transfer

practice-audit.helps: when a study or practice method may not exercise what the real task demands: practice transfers best when it calls for the same kind of response as the target, and transfer to a different skill is rare; the four-question audit itself is untested craft
practice-audit.backfires: when "resemble the target" is read as copying its surface conditions: varying practice conditions often improves retention, and context effects fade when practice does not rely on the surroundings

claims.claim: Deliberately writing out a situation from another party's point of view reduces egocentric bias, and brings out considerations the writer would otherwise miss, compared with considering it only from one's own view.
Imagining another person's perspective does not reliably make you more accurate about what they think. Asking them does.
Reflecting on one's own situation from a distanced perspective (third person, or "me in a year") reduces emotional reactivity and supports wiser reasoning, compared with a first-person immersed view.
Physically placing a figure at, or standing in, another party's position increases adoption of that party's perspective, compared with imagining it.

perspective-swap.helps: when you are stuck in your own view of a situation that involves other people: writing it from their side reduces self-centred judgement and, in negotiation studies, surfaced deals people had missed, but it does not make you more accurate about what they think, so close by writing what you would ask them; the self-distanced role gives only a small lift
perspective-swap.backfires: when the other side is a competitor, since considering their view can make people act more selfishly, when you slip into a stereotype of the role, or when the imagined view is read back as their actual view, which can raise confidence without raising accuracy

claims.claim: Monitoring progress towards a goal increases goal attainment, and more so when the progress is physically recorded.

People recall their earlier attitudes, feelings or confidence as closer to their present state than they were, or as fitting their theory of how they must have changed. A written baseline is therefore needed to see real change.
claims.construct: consistency and change biases in autobiographical memory (implicit theories of stability and change)

claims.claim: Writing about emotional experiences produces small improvements in wellbeing and health outcomes compared with neutral writing.
Leaving a visible cue of where you were and what comes next at the point of interruption reduces the time and errors involved in resuming a task.

check-in.helps: when you want to see change over weeks: the same rows written each week are progress monitoring, which gives a small lift to goal attainment, and they keep a baseline your memory would otherwise rewrite; the free-write adds at most a small lift
check-in.backfires: when the rows turn into scores to hit, since rewards tied to a monitored target undermine interest, when the free-write stirs up distress (emotional writing raises it in the short term), or when the ritual becomes a chore and is dropped

claims.claim: Writing out a dreaded outcome concretely, including what would happen next and how one would cope, lowers its felt severity. People overestimate how bad and how long-lasting their reaction to negative events will be.
claims.construct: decatastrophising (cognitive therapy); the impact bias and immune neglect in affective forecasting

claims.claim: People recall their earlier attitudes, feelings or confidence as closer to their present state than they were, or as fitting their theory of how they must have changed. A written baseline is therefore needed to see real change.
claims.construct: consistency and change biases in autobiographical memory (implicit theories of stability and change)

worst-case.helps: when a dread belongs to no plan: people overestimate how long a bad outcome will hurt, and in forecasting studies thinking about everything else that will fill the following days reduced that overestimate; the before and after ratings show whether the page did the same for you
worst-case.backfires: when the next-day, week and month block only rehearses the catastrophe, without the other things that will fill those days, which may feed worry (untested), or when defusing the dread makes a real risk feel acceptable

claims.claim: Forming written if-then plans ("When situation X arises, I will do Y") increases goal attainment compared with forming a goal intention alone.
Telling others about an identity-relevant intention can substitute for acting on it, reducing the effort invested compared with keeping it private.

commit.helps: when the goal is already decided and the gap is acting on it: one written if-then plan, tied to a cue you will actually meet and as specific as a day and time, raises follow-through for a single goal
commit.backfires: when one page carries plans for many goals at once, which draws attention to how hard they all are and weakens commitment, and when an identity goal is announced to people who will merely notice it, which can feel like progress already made, so the "Who I will tell" line stays off by default

claims.claim: Contrasting a desired future with the inner obstacle that stands in its way, then planning how to meet that obstacle (MCII / WOOP), increases goal attainment compared with positive fantasising, dwelling on obstacles, or planning alone.
Forming written if-then plans ("When situation X arises, I will do Y") increases goal attainment compared with forming a goal intention alone.

mental-contrast.helps: when a wish is one you can realistically reach: setting the outcome against the inner obstacle, then writing an if-then plan for that obstacle, gives a small but consistent lift to follow-through, a little smaller on paper than with a guide
mental-contrast.backfires: when the Obstacle box is skipped and the page becomes pure positive fantasy, which lowers effort, and when success is unlikely, where contrasting is meant to lead you to let the wish go, so ending in disengagement is the page working, not failing

claims.claim: Breaking a task into its ordered component steps before predicting when it will be done reduces optimistic bias in completion-time predictions.

timeline.helps: when a task has many parts and you are tempted to guess its end date whole: writing the steps out in order makes the work visible before you commit to a time, though no study tests ordering steps as this page does
timeline.backfires: when the steps turn into a story of how everything will go right, since plan-focused scenarios are what make time predictions too optimistic, and when the finish date is set without comparing it with how long similar work took before

claims.claim: Setting a fixed time limit for a phase of work ends deliberation sooner, with no loss of decision quality for convergent tasks.
Time pressure during idea generation reduces creative, divergent output.
claims.construct: time pressure and creativity (challenge vs hindrance stressors)

timer.helps: when a convergent decision is being turned over long after new information has stopped arriving: a written stop time is a craft practice for forcing a choice, not a tested method
timer.backfires: when the stop is set on idea generation, where time pressure is the known risk, or on a decision that needs every option weighed; nothing read shows a timebox leaves decision quality intact

claims.claim: People recall their earlier attitudes, feelings or confidence as closer to their present state than they were, or as fitting their theory of how they must have changed. A written baseline is therefore needed to see real change.
claims.construct: consistency and change biases in autobiographical memory (implicit theories of stability and change)

claims.claim: Monitoring progress towards a goal increases goal attainment, and more so when the progress is physically recorded.

scoresheet.helps: when a felt sense is likely to shift: writing the before rating down means the after rating is compared with what you actually said, not with a memory that drifts towards how you feel now
scoresheet.backfires: when the numbers become a target, since rewards tied to a monitored target undermine interest in the activity, and when the visible before rating anchors the after one; whether hiding it helps is untested

claims.claim: Deliberately testing a feared prediction with a small, planned real-world action, and then comparing what happened with what was expected, reduces avoidance and revises the expectation. The comparison step is doing work, not just the exposure.
claims.construct: behavioural experiments; expectancy violation (inhibitory learning); mastery experiences (self-efficacy)

small-experiment.helps: when an aversion rests on a prediction you can test cheaply: writing the prediction down, running one small safe probe and comparing the result at the return follows how exposure work is structured, which helps when self-guided but less than with a guide; the comparison step's own contribution is untested
small-experiment.backfires: when it is used on a diagnosed anxiety problem, which it does not treat, when the probe is too big to feel safe, or when the result is never set against the prediction; whether an unguided probe can make the fear worse is untested

claims.claim: A persistent behaviour often serves several goals at once. Listing the goals it serves before looking for alternatives yields replacements that are more likely to be adopted than replacements aimed at its stated goal alone.
claims.construct: multifinality (goal systems theory); functional assessment and functionally equivalent replacement behaviour

goal-factoring.helps: when a habit keeps resisting replacement: listing what it does for you before looking for other means is untested craft, adapted from functional assessment, which works when a practitioner does it for someone else
goal-factoring.backfires: when the list of goals is a story made up after the fact rather than what the habit really serves; no study tests factoring your own behaviour

claims.claim: A checklist or reference card kept at hand reduces omissions in multi-step or rule-governed tasks compared with relying on memory.

return-checklist.helps: when a return has steps that are easy to forget; a checklist is meant to catch omissions, but the checklist evidence comes from clinical and cockpit procedures, not from sending pages back
return-checklist.backfires: when boxes get ticked without the steps being done

claims.claim: Reading on paper yields better comprehension than reading the same text on a screen, especially for expository text read under time limits.

People reviewing automated or AI output accept its errors at elevated rates, both acting on wrong outputs (commission) and missing unflagged problems (omission). Interventions that force active evaluation reduce this overreliance.
claims.construct: automation bias and complacency; cognitive forcing

sheet.helps: when an expository text has to be understood, not skimmed: reading on paper gives slightly better comprehension than reading on screen, a small effect, largest for informational text
sheet.backfires: when the job is hunting for typos and slips, which the one error-detection study found easier on screen, or when the page is read without actively checking each point, which lets an AI draft's errors through

claims.claim: People reviewing automated or AI output accept its errors at elevated rates, both acting on wrong outputs (commission) and missing unflagged problems (omission). Interventions that force active evaluation reduce this overreliance.
claims.construct: automation bias and complacency; cognitive forcing

claims.claim: Reading on paper yields better comprehension than reading the same text on a screen, especially for expository text read under time limits.
A fixed, shared set of marks, each mapped to one editing action, is used reliably by writers and editors to communicate corrections on paper.
claims.construct: proofreaders' marks as a mark → action convention

proof.helps: when an AI draft needs checking point by point: a number and a margin on every paragraph invite an active judgement on each, and paper gives slightly better comprehension of expository text
proof.backfires: when marking turns into rubber-stamping every paragraph, or when the job is catching surface typos, which one study found easier on screen

claims.claim: Imagining that an outcome has already happened ("it failed") leads people to generate more, and more specific, reasons for it than imagining that it might happen.
Running a pre-mortem on a plan reduces overconfidence in it and surfaces more risks than a standard critique or pros-and-cons review.
claims.construct: the pre-mortem as a debiasing technique

pre-mortem/iterate.helps: when one round of failure reasons still leaves you unsure; each round inherits the pre-mortem's evidence, but the surprise gate that decides whether to run another is a design choice, and no study says a round lowers the odds by any amount
pre-mortem/iterate.backfires: when each extra round forces out more reasons, since listing many is hard and that difficulty can make failure feel less likely, or when explaining imagined failures in detail inflates how probable they seem

claims.claim: Distributing a fixed budget of tokens across options makes trade-offs and opportunity costs explicit, and yields more differentiated priorities than rating each option independently.
claims.construct: constant-sum allocation vs. independent ratings; opportunity-cost neglect

claims.claim: Effort towards a goal increases as the remaining distance to it shrinks, and making the remaining distance visible strengthens the effect.
claims.construct: the goal-gradient effect; perceived goal distance

claims.claim: Physically rearranging external objects to think, rather than to reach a physical goal, reduces the cognitive cost of a problem and improves or speeds its solution compared with manipulating the same elements mentally.
claims.construct: epistemic action; interactivity in problem solving

tokens/countdown.helps: when a Series or Ritual arc has a fixed number of sessions left and nearer milestones sit beside the count; effort tends to rise as a goal gets close, which the shrinking pile makes visible, though this has not been tested without an external reward
tokens/countdown.backfires: when many sessions remain, since motivation tends to dip in the middle of the distance, or when a nearly empty pile invites coasting before the arc is done

claims.claim: Writing down a duration estimate before a task and comparing it with the actual duration afterwards reduces later underestimation, because people otherwise misremember how long past tasks took.
claims.construct: the planning fallacy; memory bias for past durations; feedback on estimates

claims.claim: After an outcome is known, people misremember their earlier probability estimates as closer to the outcome than they were. A dated, written prediction removes that memory distortion when the forecast is scored.
claims.construct: hindsight bias (the memory-design "I knew it" effect)

claims.claim: Making explicit probability forecasts and then receiving outcome feedback or scores improves calibration over successive rounds.
claims.construct: calibration training; forecasting with scoring rules

claims.claim: Breaking a task into its ordered component steps before predicting when it will be done reduces optimistic bias in completion-time predictions.

forecast/duration.helps: when a day's tasks can be estimated before starting and timed as they finish; people underestimate durations partly because they misremember how long past tasks took, but the evidence that seeing actual durations improves later estimates is mixed, and it seems to help most when the next task is like the last
forecast/duration.backfires: when the actual times go unrecorded, so the next estimate leans on a memory that runs short, or when past overruns are explained away as one-offs, which is how people keep discounting their own track record

claims.claim: Retrieving studied material from memory (for example, writing down everything you can recall with the book closed) improves retention at a delay of days or more, compared with spending the same time restudying it.

Checking recall against the source right after retrieving it increases the retention benefit and corrects errors that would otherwise persist. Without feedback, errors produced during recall tend to be retained.
claims.construct: feedback in test-enhanced learning; self-scoring accuracy

claims.claim: Errors a person made with high confidence are more likely to be corrected on a later test, once feedback is seen, than errors made with low confidence.

Coarse, three-level confidence ratings discriminate correct from incorrect judgements above chance (resolution), even though people are typically overconfident in absolute terms. Items marked low-confidence are therefore a useful flag for risk.

free-recall/with-confidence.helps: when some recalled answers feel certain: errors made with high confidence are the ones most readily corrected once checked, and the dots show which corrections matter most
free-recall/with-confidence.backfires: when a correction is not revisited: a week later, corrected high-confidence errors were the likeliest to come back

claims.claim: Retrieving studied material from memory (for example, writing down everything you can recall with the book closed) improves retention at a delay of days or more, compared with spending the same time restudying it.

Checking recall against the source right after retrieving it increases the retention benefit and corrects errors that would otherwise persist. Without feedback, errors produced during recall tend to be retained.
claims.construct: feedback in test-enhanced learning; self-scoring accuracy

claims.claim: Trying to answer questions about material before studying it, even when most answers are wrong, improves later retention of that material compared with studying it without a pretest.

free-recall/cued.helps: when used before first studying a text: attempting the prompts first, even with wrong answers, improves later memory for the prompted material, provided the answers are then studied
free-recall/cued.backfires: when the answers are never studied afterwards, or when the prompts narrow reading to the prompted parts, which studies of reading (though not of video) have reported

claims.claim: Prompting learners to explain to themselves why each step of given material follows improves understanding and transfer, compared with studying the same material without such prompts.

For novices, studying worked examples whose final steps are progressively removed (completion problems) improves learning compared with unaided problem solving. The advantage shrinks or reverses as expertise grows.
claims.construct: the worked-example effect with fading, and the expertise-reversal effect

self-explain/faded.helps: when the procedure is new to you: removing worked steps from the end helped near transfer more than pairing examples with problems, in a few studies
self-explain/faded.backfires: when you already know the procedure: techniques that help novices can lose their benefit, or hurt, for more experienced learners (expertise reversal)

claims.claim: Prompting learners to explain to themselves why each step of given material follows improves understanding and transfer, compared with studying the same material without such prompts.
Prompting learners to answer "why is this true?" for stated facts improves recall of those facts compared with reading them.

self-explain/why.helps: when you already know something about the topic: answering "why is this true?" for facts is rated a moderately useful technique, on limited evidence
self-explain/why.backfires: when the topic is new to you, so the "why" answers have little to draw on

claims.claim: Monitoring progress towards a goal increases goal attainment, and more so when the progress is physically recorded.

People recall their earlier attitudes, feelings or confidence as closer to their present state than they were, or as fitting their theory of how they must have changed. A written baseline is therefore needed to see real change.
claims.construct: consistency and change biases in autobiographical memory (implicit theories of stability and change)

claims.claim: Writing about emotional experiences produces small improvements in wellbeing and health outcomes compared with neutral writing.
Regularly writing down things one is grateful for produces small improvements in well-being. Weekly writing is at least as effective as daily.
claims.construct: gratitude interventions; hedonic adaptation to repeated positive activities

check-in/gratitude.helps: when you want the weekly page to note something that went well: a short gratitude list raised positive mood in controlled studies that used weekly or daily lists, and any gain is likely small
check-in/gratitude.backfires: when gratitude is forced or rote, or treated as a remedy for low mood, which is why the row is optional and off by default; its benefit over other positive writing is not established

claims.claim: People recall their earlier attitudes, feelings or confidence as closer to their present state than they were, or as fitting their theory of how they must have changed. A written baseline is therefore needed to see real change.
claims.construct: consistency and change biases in autobiographical memory (implicit theories of stability and change)

claims.claim: Monitoring progress towards a goal increases goal attainment, and more so when the progress is physically recorded.
Rating satisfaction in several named life domains gives a reliable and valid measure of subjective well-being, and it shows which domain drives a change that a single overall rating hides.
claims.construct: domain satisfaction; the Personal Wellbeing Index; bottom-up models of life satisfaction

sources.cite: International Wellbeing Group (2013), Personal Wellbeing Index manual

scoresheet/domains.helps: when you want to see which part of life moved between returns: rating named domains follows an established well-being measure whose answers are stable over weeks and change little with rating order; the page measures, it does not improve anything
scoresheet/domains.backfires: when the domains change from one return to the next, when an average is allowed to hide the one domain that matters, or when the ratings are read as a score to raise

claims.claim: Forming written if-then plans ("When situation X arises, I will do Y") increases goal attainment compared with forming a goal intention alone.
Deciding a class of repeated choices together, as a rule or policy, produces more consistent and more farsighted choices than deciding each instance separately.
claims.construct: broad vs narrow choice bracketing; bundling of choices; personal rules

claims.claim: Telling others about an identity-relevant intention can substitute for acting on it, reducing the effort invested compared with keeping it private.

commit/policy.helps: when the same choice keeps coming back: deciding the rule and its named exceptions once, before the next instance, may tilt the choices towards the long-term option, though the one experiment behind this found the shift only in people who usually take the short-term one
commit/policy.backfires: when the rule bundles choices better made fresh each time (people choosing many at once pick more variety than they later want), and when a rigid rule, once broken, is dropped altogether, a risk that is theory rather than tested

claims.claim: A persistent behaviour often serves several goals at once. Listing the goals it serves before looking for alternatives yields replacements that are more likely to be adopted than replacements aimed at its stated goal alone.
claims.construct: multifinality (goal systems theory); functional assessment and functionally equivalent replacement behaviour

claims.claim: Deliberately testing a feared prediction with a small, planned real-world action, and then comparing what happened with what was expected, reduces avoidance and revises the expectation. The comparison step is doing work, not just the exposure.
claims.construct: behavioural experiments; expectancy violation (inhibitory learning); mastery experiences (self-efficacy)

goal-factoring/aversion.helps: when an activity is avoided for reasons you cannot yet name: splitting it into parts and giving each a verdict before any fix is untested craft, and the internal fixes it hands to small-experiment carry that page's cautions
goal-factoring/aversion.backfires: when the verdicts are rationalisations rather than what actually puts you off, or when an internal fix is tried as a probe too large to feel safe

claims.claim: Items placed inside the same bounded region are perceived as belonging together, even against other grouping cues, so labelled zones make category membership readable at a glance.
claims.construct: the Gestalt principle of common region (perceptual grouping)

claims.claim: Keeping task-relevant information in a stable, visible external store, rather than in working memory, improves performance on the concurrent task, at the cost of weaker memory for the offloaded content.
Leaving a visible cue of where you were and what comes next at the point of interruption reduces the time and errors involved in resuming a task.

dashboard.helps: when a session has several pieces of state to hold at once (the current decision, open questions, time left); keeping them in view frees working memory in reminder and saving studies, and items in one box tend to be read as a group
dashboard.backfires: when the boxes are not kept current, since offloading helps only while the store can be trusted, or when something offloaded is needed later without the page, because people remember less of what they expect to be able to look up

claims.claim: Placing items on a spatial layout defined by two explicit dimensions makes their relative standing on both dimensions easier to judge and compare than a list or table does.
People prefer tasks framed as urgent (short completion windows) over important tasks with objectively larger payoffs. Separating urgency from importance should therefore counter that bias.
Items placed inside the same bounded region are perceived as belonging together, even against other grouping cues, so labelled zones make category membership readable at a glance.
claims.construct: the Gestalt principle of common region (perceptual grouping)

eisenhower.helps: when urgent-looking tasks keep crowding out important ones; people pick spuriously urgent tasks over better-paying ones, a small but replicated effect, though the grid as a fix and its four actions are untested craft
eisenhower.backfires: when urgency is rated from how pressing a task feels rather than from its real deadline, since spurious urgency is exactly what pulls choices, or when an axis does not discriminate and everything crowds one quadrant

claims.claim: Placing items on a spatial layout defined by two explicit dimensions makes their relative standing on both dimensions easier to judge and compare than a list or table does.
Items placed inside the same bounded region are perceived as belonging together, even against other grouping cues, so labelled zones make category membership readable at a glance.
claims.construct: the Gestalt principle of common region (perceptual grouping)

swot.helps: when a situation's internal and external factors need sorting into four boxes; it inherits the two-by-two's untested diagram craft and adds no evidence of its own
swot.backfires: when the boxes fill with long, general lists that are never prioritised, or when a factor that is both a strength and a weakness is forced into one box

claims.claim: Placing items on a spatial layout defined by two explicit dimensions makes their relative standing on both dimensions easier to judge and compare than a list or table does.
Items placed inside the same bounded region are perceived as belonging together, even against other grouping cues, so labelled zones make category membership readable at a glance.
claims.construct: the Gestalt principle of common region (perceptual grouping)

claims.claim: Breaking a task into its ordered component steps before predicting when it will be done reduces optimistic bias in completion-time predictions.

impact-effort.helps: when choosing what to do first among many options; it inherits the two-by-two's untested diagram craft, so treat each placement as an estimate to question
impact-effort.backfires: when effort is placed from optimistic guesses, since people routinely underestimate how long their own tasks take, so supposed quick wins crowd the low-effort side

claims.claim: Placing items on a spatial layout defined by two explicit dimensions makes their relative standing on both dimensions easier to judge and compare than a list or table does.
Items placed inside the same bounded region are perceived as belonging together, even against other grouping cues, so labelled zones make category membership readable at a glance.
claims.construct: the Gestalt principle of common region (perceptual grouping)

power-interest.helps: when mapping who can affect a plan and how much they care; it inherits the two-by-two's untested diagram craft and adds no evidence of its own
power-interest.backfires: when people's power or interest is guessed rather than checked, or when an axis does not discriminate and everyone crowds one quadrant

claims.claim: Items placed inside the same bounded region are perceived as belonging together, even against other grouping cues, so labelled zones make category membership readable at a glance.
claims.construct: the Gestalt principle of common region (perceptual grouping)

claims.claim: Assigning categories to fixed places on a surface lets people keep track of and retrieve which items belong where with less effort than holding the categories in mind or in a list.

Physically rearranging external objects to think, rather than to reach a physical goal, reduces the cognitive cost of a problem and improves or speeds its solution compared with manipulating the same elements mentally.
claims.construct: epistemic action; interactivity in problem solving

playmat.helps: when several live threads need a fixed place on the table (inbox, doing, done, parked) and moving a piece records a change of state; space works as an external memory, but its advantage over a list is untested
playmat.backfires: when the four stages do not fit the work, so the mat freezes a false taxonomy, or when moving a piece stands in for deciding what to do with it

claims.claim: Items placed inside the same bounded region are perceived as belonging together, even against other grouping cues, so labelled zones make category membership readable at a glance.
claims.construct: the Gestalt principle of common region (perceptual grouping)

now-next-later.helps: when a list of work needs sorting by horizon and "later" is allowed to stay vague; the preset adds no claim beyond the zones
now-next-later.backfires: when "next" becomes a second "now" and nothing is truly deferred

claims.claim: Items placed inside the same bounded region are perceived as belonging together, even against other grouping cues, so labelled zones make category membership readable at a glance.
claims.construct: the Gestalt principle of common region (perceptual grouping)

start-stop-continue.helps: when looking back over a stretch of work and the changes need sorting into three plain verbs; the preset adds no claim beyond the zones
start-stop-continue.backfires: when the zones collect complaints rather than behaviours someone will actually change

claims.claim: Items placed inside the same bounded region are perceived as belonging together, even against other grouping cues, so labelled zones make category membership readable at a glance.
claims.construct: the Gestalt principle of common region (perceptual grouping)

kanban.helps: when work moves through stages and seeing what is in progress matters more than the plan; the preset adds no claim beyond the zones
kanban.backfires: when "doing" fills up without a limit, or moving cards across the board replaces finishing them

claims.claim: Items placed inside the same bounded region are perceived as belonging together, even against other grouping cues, so labelled zones make category membership readable at a glance.
claims.construct: the Gestalt principle of common region (perceptual grouping)

business-model-canvas.helps: when a business idea needs its parts laid out side by side so that gaps and contradictions show; the preset adds no claim beyond the zones
business-model-canvas.backfires: when filling every box feels like validation: a complete canvas is a set of guesses, not tested evidence

claims.claim: Items placed inside the same bounded region are perceived as belonging together, even against other grouping cues, so labelled zones make category membership readable at a glance.
claims.construct: the Gestalt principle of common region (perceptual grouping)

lean-canvas.helps: when an early product idea needs its problem, customer, and riskiest assumption on one page; the preset adds no claim beyond the zones
lean-canvas.backfires: when filling every box feels like validation: a complete canvas is a set of guesses, not tested evidence

claims.claim: Setting a creative problem aside for a break, then returning to it, increases solutions or ideas compared with working on it continuously for the same total time.
Sleeping between first exposure to a problem and a later retest increases the likelihood of discovering a hidden solution or rule, compared with an equal period awake.
Walking, compared with sitting, increases divergent-thinking output during the walk and shortly after it.
claims.construct: walking / acute physical activity and divergent thinking

claims.claim: Separating idea generation from evaluation, with judgement deferred until generation is done, increases the number of ideas without reducing, and sometimes increasing, the number of good ones.
Time pressure during idea generation reduces creative, divergent output.
claims.construct: time pressure and creativity (challenge vs hindrance stressors)

claims.claim: Incubation benefits are larger (a) after a longer preparation period, (b) with longer breaks up to a point, and (c) when the break is filled with a low-demand activity rather than rest or a demanding task.

incubation.helps: when an open-ended problem has been worked properly before the break and the break is spent on something easy and different; across studies a break helps on average, more for divergent tasks than for insight puzzles
incubation.backfires: when preparation was too short, when the break is filled with demanding work, or when the problem is easy or well-structured: sleep helped mainly on hard problems, and walking lifted divergent but not convergent thinking

claims.claim: Retrieving studied material from memory (for example, writing down everything you can recall with the book closed) improves retention at a delay of days or more, compared with spending the same time restudying it.
Spreading the same amount of study or retrieval across sessions separated by days produces better long-term retention than massing it into one session.
Opening a study session by retrieving earlier material before restudying it improves learning from the restudy that follows, compared with restudying first.
Trying to answer questions about material before studying it, even when most answers are wrong, improves later retention of that material compared with studying it without a pretest.

For a fixed retention interval, the gap between sessions that maximises retention is a fraction of that interval, and that fraction shrinks as the interval grows. For a target of about one month, gaps of about 1, 3 and 7 days fall in or near the high-retention region.
claims.construct: the spacing lag × retention interval interaction (the "temporal ridgeline")

claims.claim: An expanding schedule of retrieval gaps (for example 1d → 3d → 7d) produces better long-term retention than a uniform schedule with the same total spacing.

Retrieving items to a criterion across several spaced sessions, and dropping or targeting items according to the previous session's failures, gives durable retention. Returns diminish after about three relearning sessions.

Interleaving practice across confusable categories or problem types improves later discrimination and problem solving compared with blocked practice. The benefit shrinks, or reverses, for dissimilar categories and for verbal or expository material.

series.helps: when material has to be remembered for weeks: recalling it across sessions days apart, and recalling before rereading, beats massing the same study into one sitting
series.backfires: when sessions bunch together or the first recall comes too soon after study, when word lists or notes from unrelated categories are mixed in one round, or when the schedule is dropped for cramming because massed study feels more effective

claims.claim: Monitoring progress towards a goal increases goal attainment, and more so when the progress is physically recorded.

People recall their earlier attitudes, feelings or confidence as closer to their present state than they were, or as fitting their theory of how they must have changed. A written baseline is therefore needed to see real change.
claims.construct: consistency and change biases in autobiographical memory (implicit theories of stability and change)

claims.claim: Writing about emotional experiences produces small improvements in wellbeing and health outcomes compared with neutral writing.
Leaving a visible cue of where you were and what comes next at the point of interruption reduces the time and errors involved in resuming a task.
Monitoring and reflecting once a week is frequent enough to obtain most of the benefit of progress monitoring, without the adherence drop-off of daily monitoring.
A reflective writing session of ten minutes or less is enough to obtain the benefits of monitoring and reflective writing.
claims.construct: dose in expressive writing and reflection

ritual.helps: when the same question is worth coming back to: an identical page at each return is progress monitoring on paper, a small but real help, and keeps a written baseline memory cannot quietly revise, while the weekly cadence and the ten-minute length are design choices, not tested doses
ritual.backfires: when the return becomes a chore and is abandoned, when the rows turn into targets, or when the Saving State line is vague, since a cue that no longer matches where you were can slow resumption more than no cue

claims.claim: Forming written if-then plans ("When situation X arises, I will do Y") increases goal attainment compared with forming a goal intention alone.
Setting a fixed time limit for a phase of work ends deliberation sooner, with no loss of decision quality for convergent tasks.
Having one's smartphone within reach, even silent and face down, reduces available cognitive capacity, and moving it to another room restores that capacity.
claims.construct: the "brain drain" / mere-presence effect of smartphones

claims.claim: Ending a work session in the middle of a unit of work, such as mid-sentence, rather than at a natural break, increases the likelihood and ease of resuming the work at the next session.
claims.construct: the resumption tendency after interruption (Ovsiankina effect); the Zeigarnik effect

claims.claim: Leaving a visible cue of where you were and what comes next at the point of interruption reduces the time and errors involved in resuming a task.
Switching between tasks carries a measurable time and accuracy cost compared with staying on one task. Doing one kind of thinking at a time avoids that cost.
A single focused working session of about 40 minutes can be sustained without a marked decline in attention or quality for self-directed thinking work.
claims.construct: sustained attention over a session; vigilance decrement; mental fatigue

sitting.helps: when one block of thinking work needs a set start and end: a written if-then plan for when you will sit has good evidence behind it, while the timebox, the 40-minute length and the ten-page limit are design choices
sitting.backfires: when the timebox is enforced on work that is still generating ideas, when too many moves are squeezed into one block, and when moving the phone away is treated as proven: the best-known brain-drain result failed a pre-registered replication

claims.claim: People reviewing automated or AI output accept its errors at elevated rates, both acting on wrong outputs (commission) and missing unflagged problems (omission). Interventions that force active evaluation reduce this overreliance.
claims.construct: automation bias and complacency; cognitive forcing

claims.claim: Reading on paper yields better comprehension than reading the same text on a screen, especially for expository text read under time limits.
A fixed, shared set of marks, each mapped to one editing action, is used reliably by writers and editors to communicate corrections on paper.
claims.construct: proofreaders' marks as a mark → action convention

claims.claim: Keeping each mark's or colour's meaning constant across contexts leads to faster, more accurate use than mappings that change with context, which provoke mode errors.
claims.construct: consistent vs varied mapping (automaticity); mode errors

proof.helps: when an AI draft needs checking point by point: marking every paragraph forces an active judgement on each, which reduced overreliance on AI in one experiment, and paper gives slightly better comprehension of expository text; the mark conventions themselves are untested craft
proof.backfires: when marking turns into rubber-stamping, when the forcing step feels onerous enough to skip (users rated the most effective forcing designs least favourably), or when the job is catching surface errors, which one study found easier on screen

claims.claim: Coarse, three-level confidence ratings discriminate correct from incorrect judgements above chance (resolution), even though people are typically overconfident in absolute terms. Items marked low-confidence are therefore a useful flag for risk.

Coding a category in two channels at once, colour plus letter or glyph, keeps it identifiable when one channel fails (colour-vision deficiency, poor light, a mono print or photo) and improves identification over colour alone.
claims.construct: redundant coding (redundancy gain); accessibility of colour use

sources.cite: W3C, WCAG 2.1 Success Criterion 1.4.1 "Use of Color" (2018)

claims.claim: Errors a person made with high confidence are more likely to be corrected on a later test, once feedback is seen, than errors made with low confidence.

confidence-dots.helps: when many items need a quick certainty mark so the agent can see where doubt lies; confidence tracks accuracy above chance in general, but a three-level dot scale is untested, so read the dots as relative flags, not probabilities
confidence-dots.backfires: when a high dot is taken as settled, since excess certainty persists even where other overconfidence fades, or when the mark relies on colour alone and is lost to colour-blindness or a poor photo

claims.claim: Colour-coding items by category speeds finding the items of a target category and improves accuracy, compared with uncoded material, when the reader knows the code. The benefit falls as the number of colours grows.

Coding a category in two channels at once, colour plus letter or glyph, keeps it identifiable when one channel fails (colour-vision deficiency, poor light, a mono print or photo) and improves identification over colour alone.
claims.construct: redundant coding (redundancy gain); accessibility of colour use

sources.cite: W3C, WCAG 2.1 Success Criterion 1.4.1 "Use of Color" (2018)

claims.claim: Keeping each mark's or colour's meaning constant across contexts leads to faster, more accurate use than mappings that change with context, which provoke mode errors.
claims.construct: consistent vs varied mapping (automaticity); mode errors

colour-language.helps: when the ink colours carry a small, fixed set of meanings the reader already knows, and each role also carries its letter, so the meaning survives a mono print, colour-blindness or a bad photo
colour-language.backfires: when there are more colours than a reader can reliably tell apart, when the letter is skipped once coloured pens are to hand, or when marking in colour is mistaken for learning rather than a way to find things again: colour coding helps search under some conditions and hurts under others

claims.claim: A fixed, shared set of marks, each mapped to one editing action, is used reliably by writers and editors to communicate corrections on paper.
claims.construct: proofreaders' marks as a mark → action convention

claims.claim: Keeping each mark's or colour's meaning constant across contexts leads to faster, more accurate use than mappings that change with context, which provoke mode errors.
claims.construct: consistent vs varied mapping (automaticity); mode errors

proof-actions.helps: when every mark keeps one meaning on every page, following the long practice of proofreaders' marks; whether fixed marks are used reliably has not been tested
proof-actions.backfires: when a mark's or colour's meaning shifts between pages or contexts, which invites mode errors even in trained users

claims.claim: Writing by hand rather than typing improves conceptual understanding and recall of the material written.
claims.construct: longhand vs laptop note-taking; the encoding effects of handwriting

sources.cite: Van der Weel & van der Meer (2024)

collection.helps: when the page is worked by hand and the aim is to think it through in your own words; any advantage of handwriting over typing is small and contested, so no page rests on it
collection.backfires: when writing by hand slows you so much that you get less down: in note-taking studies writing more went with better scores, and the direct replication of the best-known handwriting study found no advantage
